stem: Based on the text, Okonjo would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus: Forecasters have long estimated the largest hailstones a thunderstorm can produce from the peak speed of its updraft, reasoning that faster-rising air can hold heavier ice aloft. Atmospheric scientist Liesel Okonjo argues that this measure leaves out a key factor. In her simulations, storms with broad updrafts produced larger hail than storms with narrower but faster ones, because a wide updraft keeps a growing stone suspended among supercooled droplets for longer. Speed matters, Okonjo concedes, but only together with the time a stone spends in the zone where it grows.
choices: A storm's peak updraft speed is enough on its own to predict the largest hailstones it can produce.
Two storms with equal peak updraft speeds may still produce hailstones of different maximum sizes.
The speed of a storm's updraft has no effect on the size of the hailstones that the storm produces.
Narrow updrafts keep growing hailstones suspended for longer periods than broad updrafts are able to.
explanation: Okonjo argues that hail size depends on how long a stone stays in the growth zone, which depends on updraft width, not just speed. Extend that to a new case: if two storms have the same speed but different widths, her reasoning predicts different maximum hail sizes. That is what B says.

A.why: This is the forecasters' view that Okonjo is arguing against. You picked the view the passage explains most clearly instead of isolating Okonjo's own claim that speed alone leaves out a key factor.

C.why: You pushed Okonjo's position too far. She concedes that speed matters; her claim is that it isn't the only factor, not that it plays no role.

D.why: This reverses the passage. Okonjo says that wide updrafts keep stones suspended longer, which is why broad updrafts produced larger hail in her simulations.

stem: Based on the text, Arrieta would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus: Planners often judge a new bus lane by how much it shortens the average trip. Urban researcher Tomás Arrieta contends that riders care less about average speed than about predictability. Studying twelve city corridors, he found that ridership rose most where new lanes narrowed the gap between the fastest and slowest trips, even when the average trip barely changed. A route that reliably takes twenty minutes, Arrieta argues, may attract more riders than one that averages fifteen but sometimes takes thirty.
choices: A bus lane is most likely to attract riders when it produces the largest cut in average trip time.
Average trip time has no influence on whether riders decide to use a particular bus route at all.
Ridership grew most on corridors where trip times became more variable after lanes were added.
A bus lane that narrows the range of trip times without shortening the average could raise ridership.
explanation: Arrieta's claim is that predictability drives ridership more than average speed, and his corridors showed ridership rising even when average times barely changed. Apply that to a lane that narrows the range but leaves the average alone, and his reasoning predicts more riders. That is D.

A.why: This is the planners' usual standard, the one Arrieta argues against. You chose the conventional view because the first sentence states it plainly, instead of isolating Arrieta's own claim.

B.why: Arrieta says riders care less about average speed, not that it doesn't matter at all. You turned a claim about which factor matters more into a claim that one factor doesn't count.

C.why: This reverses his finding. Ridership rose most where the spread between fast and slow trips got smaller, not larger.

stem: Based on the text, Sandoval would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus: Astronomers commonly separate giant planets from brown dwarfs by mass: objects above about 13 Jupiter masses, heavy enough to fuse deuterium, are classed as brown dwarfs. Astrophysicist Mira Sandoval argues that this cutoff hides how such objects form. Planets build up within disks of material around young stars, while brown dwarfs collapse directly from gas clouds, as stars do. Sandoval notes that both processes appear able to produce objects on either side of the 13-Jupiter-mass line, and she suggests that classifying by origin would better reflect what these objects are.
choices: An object of 15 Jupiter masses that formed within a disk around a young star could reasonably be called a planet.
Any object that is massive enough to fuse deuterium should be classified as a brown dwarf instead of a planet.
Giant planets and brown dwarfs cannot be meaningfully told apart from each other by any available criterion.
Objects that form within disks around young stars always end up with less than 13 Jupiter masses of material.
explanation: Sandoval wants to classify these objects by how they formed, and planets are the ones that build up in disks. An object that formed in a disk would therefore count as a planet under her scheme, even if its mass puts it above the 13-Jupiter-mass line. That is A, which applies her argument to a new case.

B.why: This is the mass-based cutoff that Sandoval rejects. You picked the conventional criterion because the passage explains it first and clearly.

C.why: Sandoval doesn't say the two can't be told apart. She proposes a better criterion, origin, to replace mass. You pushed 'the current test is flawed' all the way to 'no test works.'

D.why: Sandoval says both formation processes can produce objects on either side of the line, so disk-formed objects can exceed 13 Jupiter masses.

stem: Based on the text, Varga would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus: Paleobotanists often estimate ancient temperatures from fossil leaves, since in living forests the share of species with toothed leaf edges rises as climates get cooler. Paleobotanist Anneke Varga accepts this pattern but argues that temperature is not its only driver. Her survey of modern floras found that plants along rivers and lakeshores bore toothed leaves more often than nearby species on drier ground at the same temperature. Varga suggests that fossil sites formed in wet settings, which are common in the record, may therefore have been read as colder than they actually were.
choices: The share of toothed leaves in a fossil flora is by itself a dependable measure of past temperatures.
The proportion of toothed leaves in a flora is unrelated to the climate in which its plants once grew.
A temperature estimate from leaves preserved in an ancient lakebed may be lower than the true value.
Plants growing on dry ground tend to have toothed leaves more often than plants growing near water.
explanation: Varga argues that wet settings raise the share of toothed leaves, and more toothed leaves get read as a cooler climate. A lakebed is a wet setting, so by her reasoning an estimate from it could come out colder than the real temperature. That is C.

A.why: This is the standard method that Varga argues is incomplete. You chose the view the passage sets up rather than her correction to it.

B.why: Varga accepts the link between toothed leaves and cooler climates and only says temperature is not the only driver. You pushed 'one of several factors' to 'no connection at all.'

D.why: This reverses her survey result. Plants near rivers and lakes had toothed leaves more often than those on drier ground.

stem: Based on the text, Asante-Lund would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus: Linguists often treat two speech varieties as dialects of one language if their speakers can understand each other, and as separate languages if they cannot. Linguist Kwame Asante-Lund argues that this test wrongly assumes understanding runs equally in both directions. In his fieldwork, speakers of one variety understood a neighboring variety far better than its speakers understood them, largely because the first group heard the other's speech regularly on radio and in markets. Intelligibility, he concludes, reflects listeners' exposure as well as how similar two varieties are.
choices: Whether speakers understand each other reliably shows whether their varieties are separate languages.
Mutual intelligibility reveals nothing at all about how similar two speech varieties actually are.
Speakers of two neighboring varieties generally understand each other about equally well.
More contact between two communities could raise intelligibility with no change to their speech.
explanation: Asante-Lund concludes that intelligibility depends partly on exposure, not only on how similar the varieties are. Extend that: if two communities heard each other more, understanding could improve even though neither way of speaking changed. That is D.

A.why: This is the conventional intelligibility test that Asante-Lund challenges. You chose it because the passage's first sentence explains it so clearly.

B.why: He says intelligibility reflects exposure as well as similarity, so similarity still counts. You pushed 'not only similarity' to 'nothing about similarity.'

C.why: His fieldwork found the opposite: one group understood the other far better than it was understood in return.
